abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL) is a peripheral T-cell malignancy caused by human T-cell leukemia virus-1. Patients diagnosed with aggressive ATL have a poor prognosis. As response duration to conventional multiagent chemotherapy is short, upfront allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT) is recommended. As disease status at the time of allo-HCT is the primary prognostic factor, bridging therapy to allo-HCT is sometimes necessary during donor coordination. However, conventional chemotherapies are often toxic, particularly for older patients and those with inadequate hematopoietic recovery. Anti-CCR4 monoclonal antibody mogamulizumab adversely affects post-transplant survival due to the high risk of severe graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). Available data on other novel agents for ATL are limited. The present case study details an ATL patient who exhibited chemotherapy intolerance, but was successfully bridged to unrelated peripheral blood stem cell transplantation (uPBSCT) with valemetostat, a selective dual inhibitor of enhancer of zeste homolog 1 and 2. Despite severe bone marrow failure, valemetostat was well tolerated by the patient and led to successful disease control prior to uPBSCT, which is considered to have contributed to a reduced risk of post-transplant relapse and an improved prognosis. No significant adverse effects of valemetostat were observed early after transplantation, in contrast to the increased incidence of severe GVHD and non-relapse mortality reported following allo-HCT after mogamulizumab therapy. These findings suggest that valemetostat is a promising option as a bridging therapy to allo-HCT for aggressive ATL.

sec.p: Keywords: adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, human T-cell leukemia virus type 1, allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation, bridging therapy, valemetostat

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Adult T-cell leukemia and lymphoma (ATL) is a peripheral T-cell malignancy caused by human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1).1 Japan is one of several regions with a high prevalence of HTLV-1, along with the Caribbean islands, Central and South America, subtropical Africa, and the Middle East.2 Approximately 5% of HTLV-1 carriers will develop ATL during their lifetime, with over 1,000 patients being diagnosed with ATL each year in Japan.3 Patients diagnosed with aggressive ATL, classified as acute, lymphoma, or unfavorable chronic types according to the Shimoyama criteria,4 typically have a poor prognosis.5 As the duration of response to conventional multi-agent chemotherapy is short, with only approximately 10% of patients achieving long-term remission,6 an upfront allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT) is recommended for treating young (≤ 70 years) and fit patients.7 Disease status at the time of allo-HCT is the primary prognostic factor, with patients with progressive disease being associated with poor outcomes.8 Therefore, prompt donor search is warranted; unrelated donors are sought if HLA-matched sibling donors are not available. Unrelated donor coordination usually requires 3–4 months in Japan, during which bridging therapy to allo-HCT is sometimes needed. However, conventional chemotherapies are often toxic, specifically for older patients and those with inadequate hematopoietic recovery. Due to severe graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), the anti-CCR4 monoclonal antibody mogamulizumab adversely affects post-transplant survival, particularly in patients with a short interval between the last dose of treatment and allo-HCT.9 Data on other novel agents for ATL are limited. Valemetostat tosylate was recently approved in Japan for relapsed or refractory ATL.10 It is a selective dual inhibitor of enhancer of zeste homolog 1 and 2 (EZH1/2). EZH1 and EZH2 are histone methyltransferases that constitute the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), cooperatively catalyzing histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3), which is associated with transcriptional repression in ATL cells.11 Inhibition of EZH1/2 reduces H3K27me3 levels, restoring the repressed genes and exerting anti-tumor effects.12 Valemetostat has exhibited a tolerable toxicity profile and favorable efficacy in clinical trials.13–15 In a phase II study involving patients with relapsed or refractory ATL,13 valemetostat achieved an overall response rate of 48%. Treatment-emergent adverse events were manageable, with grade ≥3 events including thrombocytopenia (32%), anemia (32%), lymphopenia (16%), and neutropenia (12%). However, data on the potential positive or negative impact of valemetostat therapy on subsequent allo-HCT remain limited. We hereby report an ATL patient who was intolerant to conventional chemotherapy, but was successfully bridged to unrelated peripheral blood stem cell transplantation (uPBSCT) with valemetostat.

sec.title: CASE PRESENTATION
sec.p: A 46-year-old man with a history of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), diagnosed at the age of 7 years, was referred to a hematologist for complaints of cough and leukocytosis with abnormal lymphocytes. His Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG-PS) was 1. Results of his blood tests were as follows: white blood cell (WBC) count: 28,000/μL with 63% (17,640/μL) abnormal lymphocytes; lactate dehydrogenase (LDH): 425 IU/L; soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R): 50,500 IU/mL; corrected calcium level: 8.9 mg/dL; C-reactive protein (CRP) level: 0.32 mg/dL. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography revealed abnormal fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake in the spleen and the bilateral cervical, mesenteric, para-aortic lymph nodes (Figure 1A); moreover, anti- HTLV-1 antibodies were present, and clonal integration of HTLV-1 proviral DNA was confirmed on Southern blot hybridization of the blood. Thus, a diagnosis of acute-type ATL was made. He was classified as having an intermediate risk according to the modified ATL Prognostic Index (ATL-PI) at the time of diagnosis. Ground-glass opacity (GGO) consistent with ATL infiltration was observed in the left lung on CT. Bone marrow aspiration (BMA) revealed ATL infiltration. Although there was no evidence of T-ALL relapse, a large number of micromegakaryocytes, an absence of myeloblasts (0%), and fibrosis indicating grade 3 myelofibrosis were observed. Considering the history of prior chemotherapy (not allo-HCT) for T-ALL, these findings indicated a diagnosis of therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS). Several structural and numerical abnormalities that were more likely to be due to ATL invasion than MDS were revealed on G-banded chromosomal analysis. Prior to chemotherapy for ATL, the patient had no significant cytopenia. He was classified as very low risk in accordance with the revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS-R). Aggressive ATL was considered for determining his prognosis, and upfront allo-HCT was planned after intensive induction chemotherapy.

caption.p: (A) PET-CT findings at diagnosis and at the time of allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT). (B) Treatment course for adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and corresponding laboratory values.

sec.p: The clinical course has been depicted in Figure 1B. He was administered induction therapy with VCAP-AMP-VECP (for further information regarding the regimen, refer to the footnotes in Figure 1). ATL cells and the LDH level decreased to 10,350/μL and 305 U/L, respectively following the first cycle. However, due to severe myelosuppression, probably caused by t-MDS, VCAP-AMP-VECP was intolerable. VCAP-AMP-VECP was replaced by lenalidomide; however, the patient was intolerant to lenalidomide as well due to profound myelosuppression, leading to its discontinuation after three weeks. Restaging demonstrated stable disease, with residual nodal lesions of abnormal lymphocytes. Valemetostat was subsequently initiated for pancytopenia at a reduced dose of 50 mg/day and was increased to 100 mg/day after two weeks, which was equivalent to 200 mg/day considering the concomitant use of posaconazole. After the initiation of valemetostat therapy, the patient developed CMV viremia and gastritis, necessitating prolonged ganciclovir therapy. CMV gastritis, located on the posterior wall of the lesser curvature of the antrum, was diagnosed based on immunohistochemical staining of a mucosal biopsy specimen. Nausea and decreased appetite gradually improved with ganciclovir therapy and were therefore considered unlikely to represent gastrointestinal toxicities directly attributable to valemetostat. Valemetostat was continued for seven weeks until one week prior to the conditioning therapy. Partial remission was achieved at uPBSCT. The WBC, ATL cells, and sIL-2R levels were reduced to 200/μL, 12/μL, and 1,126 U/mL, respectively. The FDG-avid lesions disappeared (Figure 1A), and the GGO in the lung resolved. Following reduced intensity conditioning, he underwent uPBSCT from an HLA 7/8 allele-matched male donor. Neutrophil engraftment was achieved on day 14. On day 14, he developed BK virus-associated hemorrhagic cystitis, which was resolved with supportive therapy. On day 30, he developed acute GVHD (overall grade II, skin stage 1, upper GI stage 1) and was treated with topical steroids and oral beclomethasone dipropionate. At 1 month after uPBSCT, no evidence of dysplasia and ATL infiltration was observed on BMA, and G-banded chromosome analysis revealed a normal karyotype. The abnormal lymphocytes in the blood disappeared morphologically; however, flow cytometric analysis (HTLV-1 Analysis System: HAS-Flow)16 indicated the presence of measurable residual disease (MRD) as a CD4+CD7-CADM1+ ATL cell population (1.5% of CD4+ cells). Increasing MRD (11.6% of CD4+ cells) observed on HAS-Flow 2 weeks later indicated a high risk of hematologic relapse. Considering the insufficient hematopoietic recovery, a maintenance therapy with valemetostat was initiated at a reduced dose of 50 mg/day on day 43. At 3 months after uPBSCT, the HAS-Flow-based MRD remained positive, and valemetostat was increased to 200 mg/day with rapid tapering of tacrolimus. The maximum grade of treatment-emergent thrombocytopenia and anemia was 2. In addition, the patient experienced neither taste disturbances nor gastrointestinal toxicities attributable to valemetostat. There was no recurrence of CMV gastritis or GVHD-related gastritis, and valemetostat therapy was not interrupted. At 4 months after uPBSCT, the HAS-Flow-based MRD turned negative, and a complete response of ATL was achieved.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: This is the first report describing successful bridging therapy to allo-HCT with valemetostat in aggressive ATL. Despite severe myelosuppression due to t-MDS, valemetostat was well tolerated by the patient and good disease control prior to uPBSCT was achieved. Furthermore, no significant adverse effects of valemetostat were reported early after transplantation.

Bridging therapy using novel agents in ATL has not been established. Due to the high risk of severe GVHD, mogamulizumab is avoided prior to allo-HCT.9 Lenalidomide could be an option, but dose-dependent myelosuppression is problematic, particularly in patients with cytopenia. In terms of safety, brentuximab vedotin monotherapy might also be a viable option based its established in the treatment of classic Hodgkin lymphoma. However, the evidence regarding ATL is limited. There is a lack of evidence with regards to bridging therapy for the recently approved valemetostat and tucidinostat. In the Japanese phase II clinical trial (J201 study),13 none of the patients had received allo-HCT after responding to valemetostat therapy. In the multinational phase II clinical trial (U202 study),15 allo-HCT was performed on one patient in the ATL cohort after valemetostat therapy; however, transplant outcomes were unknown. Only one case report has described the cases of two patients diagnosed with refractory peripheral T-cell lymphoma, who received valemetostat therapy prior to allo-HCT, which demonstrated rapid activity and was well tolerated.17

In the present case, the patient was successfully bridged to uPBSCT with valemetostat. Although he remained transfusion-dependent until donor cell engraftment, he tolerated the standard dose of valemetostat, equivalent to 200 mg/day. He developed refractory CMV viremia and gastritis during valemetostat therapy. CMV gastritis was diagnosed by immunohistochemical staining of a mucosal biopsy specimen and was differentiated from gastrointestinal toxicities attributable to valemetostat based on the favorable therapeutic response to ganciclovir. CMV infection prophylaxis during the clinical trials (J201, U202, and J101 trials)13–15 was at the discretion of the treating physician, and 7/37 (18.9%) of non-prophylactic patients developed CMV disease. Valemetostat might exacerbate cellular immunodeficiency in ATL patients. However, prior to uPBSCT, the current patient had favorable disease control. As reported in the J201 study,13 the patient achieved tumor reduction across disease components (nodal, extra-nodal, and peripheral blood lesions). Disease status at the time of transplantation is a critical prognostic factor. Even in patients who are refractory to or intolerant of conventional chemotherapy, achieving a response with salvage therapy using valemetostat may reduce the risk of post-transplant relapse. Although data on the potential negative impact of valemetostat therapy on post-transplant outcomes remain limited, no significant adverse effects were caused by valemetostat early after transplantation, in contrast to mogamulizumab.9 Our patient demonstrated a steady hematopoietic recovery with no unexpected serious complications and also achieved a complete hematologic remission of t-MDS following uPBSCT. We restarted valemetostat as a consolidation therapy for blood MRD after uPBSCT. Due to the current lack of studies on valemetostat therapy after allo-HCT, our patient requires vigilant monitoring for ATL relapse and viral infections.

In conclusion, valemetostat might be a promising option as a bridging therapy to allo-HCT for aggressive ATL. Further studies involving a larger cohort are warranted to evaluate the safety and efficacy of valemetostat therapy prior to allo-HCT.
